summary: No fire experiment has run on the Moon, yet NASA plans habitats with oxygen-rich air (34% O2 at 8.2 psia). One-Sixth gathers NASA's reduced-gravity fire data into one cited dataset and fits two models to it. Each model had to predict Earth results it never saw before it was allowed to forecast: one passed, one passed weakly, and one failed and was dropped. A separate AI reviewer then attacked every claim, and we withdrew or weakened what it broke. What survives is a timestamped forecast: at lunar gravity and habitat pressure, thin paper-like material keeps burning down to 13.8–17.9% oxygen, far below the planned 34%. It can be scored against future tests with matching material and conditions; NASA's planned FM2 experiment provides lunar fire context.
details:
One-Sixth turns NASA's reduced-gravity fire measurements into an open, testable forecast for thin cellulose tissue at lunar gravity and habitat pressure. It includes 41 cited evidence rows, original NASA PSI test tables, two models, held-out Earth checks, a registered forecast, an interactive gravity slider, an exhibit, and a published review of our own claims.

What makes it different

Each model had to predict Earth results hidden during fitting before it could forecast. Model 2 on cellulose passed, Model 1 passed weakly, and Model 2 on thin acrylic (PMMA) failed and makes no lunar forecast. A separate AI reviewer challenged the work; we published all eight findings and withdrew or weakened the claims they broke.

How it works

In still air, buoyancy supplies the draft feeding a flame; its speed scales approximately as gravity to the one-third power. Too little draft starves the flame and too much can cause blow-off. Model 1 fits a two-sided curve in gravity. Model 2 balances radiative loss and reaction time against draft speed, with a physical pressure step. Both use rejection sampling to retain parameter sets consistent with the training observations.

Results and intended impact

NASA's short aircraft tests already bracket the lunar limit at normal pressure (14.7 psia) between 14% and 15% oxygen, about 1–2.4 percentage points below Earth. These are measurements the models reproduce, not a new prediction. For the untested combination of lunar gravity and 8.2 psia, the forecast oxygen limit is 13.8–17.9%, most likely near 15.5%, compared with planned 34% oxygen habitat air. The range covers both models and every tested variant.

The project identifies a concrete next experiment: thin cellulose, flame spreading downward in still air, at lunar gravity and 8.2 psia across 13–19% oxygen. A measurement outside the forecast range would falsify it. This helps distinguish established evidence from the pressure extrapolation that still needs testing.

Limits

The forecast covers one material class and one spread direction. Aircraft parabolas last about 20 seconds and may bias limits low. Both models extrapolate pressure and share evidence, so their agreement is not independent confirmation. This is a research forecast, not a habitat safety certification.

Tools and AI use

Python, NumPy, Pillow, plain HTML/SVG and Blender. Claude (Anthropic) retrieved NASA data and reports, extracted evidence, wrote model code, web content, slides and text, and ran a separate-context review. GPT-6 Astra (OpenAI) built the oxygen-limit figure and interactive exhibit. ChatGPT assisted with preparing this submission from the repository and Claude conversation. The team chose the approach and is responsible for the claims.
